title: A handful of beans
hook: food shrinks to almost nothing; his spine shows through his belly like a string of beads (MN 36)

segments.voice: Yesterday, appanaka, the breathless meditation: his head roaring like a blacksmith's bellows. Forcing isn't finding.

There's a stone statue in the Lahore Museum, in Pakistan, from the old region of Gandhara. A man sits cross-legged in meditation. His face is calm. But his body is barely a body. Every rib stands out. The veins run like cords over his arms. His belly has sunk back almost to his spine. It's called the Fasting Buddha, and it shows the wanderer as he would later describe himself, in the forest near Uruvela. Forcing the breath hadn't worked. So he turned to another ascetic method. Eat less. Then less. Then almost nothing.
screen: `A STATUE IN LAHORE.` → `EVERY RIB STANDS OUT.` → `EAT LESS. THEN ALMOST NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Again, the Buddha tells it himself, and he doesn't spare the details. He cut his food to a handful at a time: a little bean soup, lentils, peas. His body wasted away. His limbs became like the knotted joints of vine stems, his backside like a camel's hoof. His ribs stuck out like the rafters of an old, broken shed. The gleam of his eyes sank deep into their sockets, like the gleam of water at the bottom of a deep well. His scalp shriveled like a green gourd left in the sun. When he touched his belly, he could feel his spine, pressing through like a string of beads. When he rubbed his limbs, the hair fell out at the roots. Some who saw him said he was black, others said brown. His clear, bright skin had lost its color. Then comes the line that turns the story. By this painful practice, he says, I did not reach anything beyond ordinary human states. No special knowledge. No freedom. Just starvation. Why so much detail? Because some ascetics of his time held that the more you denied the body, the closer you came to truth. He had tried it, and he reports back plainly: it didn't work. In this story, the body isn't the enemy. It's where the practice happens.
screen: `A HANDFUL AT A TIME.` · `A SPINE LIKE A STRING OF BEADS.` · `NOTHING BEYOND THE ORDINARY.` · `THE BODY ISN'T THE ENEMY.` · then, large: `STARVING ISN'T HOLY.`

segments.voice: Picture your next meal, or if you have something to eat nearby, take one small bite and chew it much more slowly than usual: the taste arriving, the texture, the way the body leans toward it. Think of the hands that grew it, carried it and cooked it, and as you swallow, let being fed be a kindness, not a guilt. Then rest with the breath.
Dukkarakarika. The hard austerities of the wanderer's fasting, down to a handful of beans, and the proof, in his own words, that starving the body doesn't free the mind.
Your line: starving isn't holy. Your body is a friend you're feeding. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada monks and nuns eat their meals before noon under the monastic rule, eating enough to sustain practice rather than starving, and the Fasting Buddha image recalls the path the Buddha tried and set aside.

fork.setup: you've cut your food to a handful of bean soup at a time. your spine shows through your belly. has it brought freedom?
options: not yet, so eat even less.

fork.reveal: he says it plainly: by this painful practice he reached nothing beyond the ordinary. starving isn't holy.

original.note: Pali: the doing of what is hard to do, the name for the Bodhisatta's austerities.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha fasted until he found enlightenment.
what it means: he fasted almost to death, and reported that it didn't work. starving isn't holy.
what a scholar hears: MN 36 gives the similes of emaciation; the Gandhara Fasting Buddha from Sikri (Lahore Museum) depicts it; the commentaries call this period dukkarakārikā, the hard practice.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the fasting and its similes

notes: MN 36 similes paraphrased (vine joints, camel's hoof, string of beads, rafters, well, gourd, hair falling at the roots, people calling his skin black or brown). Confirm order and wording.
Fasting Buddha from Sikri, Gandhara, Lahore Museum; commonly dated 2nd–3rd century CE ('nearly two thousand years ago'). Confirm.
'Nothing beyond ordinary human states' paraphrases 'no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision'. Confirm.
The practice mentions eating: a Keeper may want a note for listeners with eating disorders or who fast for other reasons.
